questions.scenario: A 68-year-old woman has had an itchy, red and white plaque on the vulva for years that was treated as eczema. A biopsy shows large pale cells with abundant cytoplasm scattered among the keratinocytes of the epidermis, with no invasion into the dermis.
questions.lead_in: Why does the surgeon plan a wide local excision, and what is the risk if margins are narrow?
questions.stem: Why does the surgeon plan a wide local excision, and what is the risk if margins are narrow?
options: The plaque is a benign sweat gland tumor, so a wide margin prevents regrowth of a dermal nodule
The lesion is HPV related and multifocal, so wide excision removes all of the infected skin
The cells spread laterally within the epidermis, so excision may be incomplete and the disease may recur
The cells have invaded deep stroma, so a wide margin is needed to reach nodal disease
The lesion is a thin sclerotic patch, so wide excision prevents later loss of the labia
choice_rationales: A benign dermal sweat gland tumor is papillary hidradenoma and would not be managed this way.
Paget disease is not an HPV driven multifocal lesion, which describes classic VIN.
Lateral intraepidermal spread is the reason for wide margins and for recurrence.
The disease is typically confined to the epidermis, so deep stromal and nodal spread is not the usual picture.
Sclerosis and loss of labia describe lichen sclerosus, not this plaque.
questions.explanation: Step 1. Large pale cells within the epidermis in an itchy red and white plaque is vulvar (extramammary) Paget disease, an intraepithelial neoplasm. Step 2. The lecture states that Paget cells spread laterally, so excision may be incomplete and the disease may recur, which is why wide local excision is the treatment. Invasion is rare, and poor prognosis follows when it does occur.
visual_clues: The epidermis is the darker band along the top.
Several pale cells are larger than the adjacent keratinocytes.
questions.visual_target: Pale atypical cells in the epidermis
questions.tested_concept: Why does the surgeon plan a wide local excision, and what is the risk if margins are narrow?

questions.condition_overview: Extramammary Paget disease is an uncommon intraepidermal adenocarcinoma, most often on the vulva of older women, that presents as a red, scaly or eczematous, itchy plaque. Microscopically large pale cells with abundant cytoplasm and atypical nuclei are scattered singly and in nests among the keratinocytes of the epidermis, sometimes extending into skin appendages. The cells contain intracytoplasmic mucin (mucicarmine and PAS positive) and are CK7 positive, unlike squamous cells. It is usually confined to the epidermis, but some cases are associated with an underlying adnexal or visceral carcinoma, and the invasive form carries a worse prognosis. Treatment is wide excision.

questions.scenario: A 70-year-old woman has a pruritic, painful, erythematous vulvar plaque. A biopsy shows an intraepithelial proliferation of malignant cells larger than the surrounding keratinocytes with pale cytoplasm. A medical student recalls that Paget disease of the nipple is often linked to an underlying cancer.
questions.lead_in: How does this vulvar disease usually differ from Paget disease of the nipple?
questions.stem: How does this vulvar disease usually differ from Paget disease of the nipple?
options: It arises from a preexisting HPV related condyloma
It is typically an in situ intraepithelial neoplasm not associated with an underlying cancer
It is almost always associated with an underlying invasive ductal carcinoma of the breast, as in Paget disease of the nipple
It is an in situ lesion that is nearly always associated with an underlying anorectal or genitourinary adenocarcinoma
It is a premalignant lesion of keratinocytes that always progresses to squamous carcinoma if left untreated for years
choice_rationales: Condyloma is a separate HPV related exophytic lesion, not the origin of Paget cells.
The lecture states it is typically in situ and not associated with underlying cancer.
Nipple Paget disease reflects underlying ductal carcinoma, whereas this vulvar disease is typically not associated with an underlying cancer.
This disease is typically an in situ intraepithelial neoplasm not associated with an underlying cancer, so a hidden adenocarcinoma is not the rule.
Paget cells are malignant and the process is not described as a squamous precursor.
questions.explanation: Step 1. Large pale malignant cells confined to the epidermis identify vulvar Paget disease. Step 2. The lecture contrasts it with Paget disease of the nipple by noting that the vulvar form is typically in situ and not associated with underlying cancer. Cells are thought to arise from multipotent cells in the mammary-like gland ducts of vulvar skin, and invasion or metastasis is rare but carries a poor prognosis.
visual_clues: Use the level of the atypical cells and their pale cytoplasm together.
questions.visual_target: Abnormal pale population within the vulvar epidermis

questions.scenario: A pathologist examines a vulvar plaque biopsy containing scattered large pale cells in the epidermis. A histochemical stain shows bright cytoplasmic positivity in these cells but not in the neighboring keratinocytes.
questions.lead_in: What does this result indicate about the cells, and how does it affect the diagnosis?
questions.stem: What does this result indicate about the cells, and how does it affect the diagnosis?
options: Fungal hyphae in the keratin layer, which indicates candidiasis
Myoepithelial cytoplasm, which indicates papillary hidradenoma
Intracytoplasmic mucin in malignant cells, which confirms Paget disease
Glycogen in normal clear keratinocytes, which excludes neoplasia
Keratin pearls from invasive squamous carcinoma
choice_rationales: Candida is shown on PAS in the thickened keratin layer, not in epidermal cells.
Hidradenoma shows myoepithelium, which is shown with calponin, SMA, and EMA, not mucin.
Mucin positive pale cells confirm Paget disease according to the lecture.
The cells that stain are malignant and are not described as normal keratinocytes.
Keratin pearls are not the finding with intracellular mucin.
questions.explanation: Step 1. Positive cytoplasmic staining of the large pale cells with mucin stains (mucicarmine or diastase PAS) shows that the cells contain mucopolysaccharide. Step 2. The lecture states this staining confirms the diagnosis of Paget disease. The stain is positive in the atypical cells and not in the surrounding keratinocytes, which is why it helps classify the conspicuous cells.
visual_clues: Locate the pink material within individual cells rather than along the surface or in the dermis.
questions.visual_target: Bright cytoplasmic material in scattered large epidermal cells
questions.tested_concept: What does this result indicate about the cells, and how does it affect the diagnosis?

questions.tested_concept: Which precursor lesion and molecular change most likely preceded this carcinoma?
questions.visual_target: Vulvar plaque and the evidence for stromal invasion
questions.scenario: A 74-year-old woman with long-standing lichen sclerosus has a firm, ulcerated vulvar lesion. A biopsy shows irregular nests of keratinizing squamous cells in the stroma beneath the surface. The tumor is HPV negative.
questions.lead_in: Which precursor lesion and molecular change most likely preceded this carcinoma?
questions.stem: Which precursor lesion and molecular change most likely preceded this carcinoma?
options: Extramammary Paget disease with mucin positive intraepidermal cells
Differentiated vulvar intraepithelial neoplasia with p53 mutation
Classic VIN with high risk HPV type 16 and multifocal disease
Condyloma acuminatum with koilocytes and papillary stromal cores
Papillary hidradenoma with myoepithelium and no epidermal link
choice_rationales: Paget disease is an intraepithelial glandular process, not a squamous precursor.
HPV negative carcinoma in an older patient with lichen sclerosus fits differentiated VIN and p53 mutation.
Classic VIN is HPV 16 related and tends to occur in younger women, which does not fit.
Condyloma is a benign exophytic HPV lesion and is not the described precursor.
Hidradenoma is a benign sweat gland tumor and is not a carcinoma precursor.
questions.explanation: Step 1. Nests of squamous cells invading the stroma are invasive squamous cell carcinoma. Step 2. The lecture states about 70 percent of vulvar carcinomas are unrelated to HPV and arise from differentiated VIN in older women, linked to lichen sclerosus or squamous hyperplasia and p53 mutation, giving keratinized squamous carcinomas. The 30 percent related to HPV arise from classic VIN and form basaloid and warty carcinomas.
visual_clues: Irregular epithelial nests lie in the underlying stroma.
questions.ground_truth_basis: Visible findings in the cited learner image interpreted with the cited teaching pages.
questions.condition_overview: Vulvar squamous cell carcinoma has two main pathways. HPV-related tumors arise from usual-type VIN in younger women and are basaloid or warty. HPV-independent tumors arise from dVIN or lichen sclerosus in older women and are keratinizing. Keratinizing tumors show irregular nests of atypical squamous cells with keratin pearls and intercellular bridges invading dermis. Depth of invasion, tumor size, and groin node status determine stage and prognosis. Treatment is wide excision, and groin node assessment is needed when invasion exceeds 1 mm.

questions.tested_concept: Which pairing correctly separates the older patient's lesion from the younger patient's?
questions.visual_target: Vulvar plaque differential at the epithelial base
questions.scenario: A 66-year-old woman has a single white vulvar plaque next to an area of lichen sclerosus. Biopsy shows atypical cells concentrated at the base of the epithelium, while the upper layers mature normally. A resident compares her to a 30-year-old smoker with multifocal lesions and prior CIN.
questions.lead_in: Which pairing correctly separates the older patient's lesion from the younger patient's?
questions.stem: Which pairing correctly separates the older patient's lesion from the younger patient's?
options: Older patient has extramammary Paget disease, younger patient has squamous hyperplasia of the vulva
Older patient has condyloma acuminatum, younger patient has lichen sclerosus of the vulva
Older patient has HPV 16 related classic VIN, younger patient has differentiated VIN
Both have classic VIN because basal atypia is always related to HPV infection of the skin
Older has HPV negative differentiated VIN with p53 mutation, younger has HPV related classic VIN
choice_rationales: Paget disease and squamous hyperplasia do not match basal atypia with maturation.
Condyloma and lichen sclerosus are benign and do not match the biopsy descriptions.
The age and unifocal pattern are reversed in this option.
Basal atypia with preserved maturation is differentiated VIN, which is not HPV related.
The lecture ties older, unifocal, lichen sclerosus related disease to differentiated VIN with p53 mutation.
questions.explanation: Step 1. Basal atypia with maturation above, unifocal, in an older woman with lichen sclerosus is differentiated VIN (VIN simplex). Step 2. The lecture lists differentiated VIN as HPV negative, older age, unifocal, associated with inflammation, lichen sclerosus or squamous hyperplasia, and p53 mutation. Classic VIN is HPV 16 related, younger, multifocal, associated with CIN and VAIN, with lack of maturation and basaloid cells.
visual_clues: The deepest epithelial cells are conspicuously atypical while the superficial layers still mature.
questions.ground_truth_basis: Visible findings in the cited learner image interpreted with the cited teaching pages.
questions.condition_overview: Differentiated VIN is an HPV-independent precancer of the vulva that occurs in older women and is typically associated with lichen sclerosus. The atypia is confined to the basal and parabasal layers, with premature keratinization and maturing, eosinophilic superficial cells that make it easy to overlook. Mutated p53 is often present. dVIN is the usual precursor of HPV-independent keratinizing vulvar squamous cell carcinoma and progresses rapidly, so it is excised.

questions.visual_target: Which test would demonstrate the cytoplasmic material that helps classify the conspicuous cells in this epidermis?
questions.stem: Which test best demonstrates the cytoplasmic material that classifies these cells?
options: A stain for dermal collagen sclerosis in the superficial dermis
PAS for fungal hyphae in the keratin layer of the epidermis
Calponin to highlight the myoepithelium around the glands
Mucicarmine or diastase PAS for intracellular mucin
A p53 immunostain to show a nuclear mutation in the cells
choice_rationales: Collagen sclerosis is the lichen sclerosus pattern.
PAS for hyphae is a different use for candidiasis.
Calponin shows myoepithelium in hidradenoma.
Mucin stains demonstrate the cytoplasmic mucopolysaccharide of Paget cells.
p53 mutation is associated with differentiated VIN.
questions.explanation: Step 1. Large pale cells in the epidermis of an eczema like plaque are Paget cells. Step 2. The lecture states that positive cytoplasmic staining with mucicarmine or diastase PAS confirms the diagnosis because the cells contain mucopolysaccharide. Calponin is for hidradenoma and p53 relates to differentiated VIN.
visual_clues: Choose mucicarmine to demonstrate cytoplasmic mucin in the large pale intraepidermal cells.

questions.scenario: A 48-year-old woman has weight loss, tremor, and heat intolerance. Her TSH is suppressed, but a thyroid scan shows no thyroid nodule. Pelvic imaging shows a unilateral ovarian mass. The ovarian section shows round follicles filled with dense eosinophilic colloid.
questions.lead_in: Which explanation accounts for her hyperthyroid symptoms?
questions.stem: Which explanation accounts for her hyperthyroid symptoms?
options: A Krukenberg tumor is releasing mucin that mimics TSH and stimulates the thyroid gland
Functioning thyroid tissue within the ovarian monodermal teratoma is producing thyroid hormone
A granulosa cell tumor is secreting inhibin that stimulates the thyroid to make hormone
A yolk sac tumor is secreting alpha fetoprotein with thyroid stimulating activity
A dysgerminoma is producing thyroid hormone from the fibrous septa of the tumor
choice_rationales: Krukenberg tumors are metastatic signet ring tumors and do not make thyroid hormone.
Struma ovarii is a monodermal teratoma with thyroid elements that can cause hyperthyroidism.
Inhibin is a marker of granulosa cell tumor and does not stimulate the thyroid.
Alpha fetoprotein is a yolk sac marker and has no thyroid stimulating role in the lecture.
Dysgerminoma is a germ cell tumor of large primitive cells and is not thyroid tissue.
questions.explanation: Step 1. Follicles filled with colloid in an ovarian tumor are thyroid tissue, so this is struma ovarii. Step 2. The lecture lists struma ovarii among specialized monodermal teratomas, which contain only thyroid elements (follicles and colloid), and notes that they may cause hyperthyroidism. A suppressed TSH with a normal thyroid gland fits an ectopic source.
visual_clues: Look for the thin cellular rims around the dense pink centers.
questions.visual_target: Rounded follicles containing dense colloid
questions.tested_concept: Which explanation accounts for her hyperthyroid symptoms?
questions.ground_truth_basis: Supplied lecture page and visible evidence on the selected image.
questions.condition_overview: Struma ovarii is a monodermal form of ovarian teratoma composed predominantly (more than half) of mature thyroid tissue. It forms thyroid follicles filled with eosinophilic colloid, and it can rarely cause hyperthyroidism or undergo malignant change. Most cases are benign and are treated by surgical resection.

questions.scenario: A 40-year-old woman has a unilateral ovarian mass removed. The pathologist reports that most of the tumor is mature thyroid follicles with colloid and cannot find skin, cartilage, or neural tissue after thorough sampling.
questions.lead_in: How should this tumor be classified within the ovarian tumor groups?
questions.stem: How should this tumor be classified within the ovarian tumor groups?
options: A specialized, monodermal teratoma, a type of germ cell tumor
A dysgerminoma analogous to seminoma, a germ cell tumor of large primitive cells in sheets separated by lymphoid septa
A sex cord stromal tumor that is feminizing
An immature teratoma, a germ cell tumor with primitive neuroepithelial tubules and malignant behavior in young women
A metastatic signet ring tumor from the stomach
choice_rationales: Germ cell tumors that differentiate along one line include struma ovarii as a monodermal teratoma.
Dysgerminoma shows sheets of large primitive cells with lymphoid septa, whereas this tumor is made almost entirely of thyroid follicles.
Sex cord stromal tumors such as granulosa cell tumor are composed of stroma and sex cord elements.
Immature teratoma shows primitive neuroepithelial tissue, which was not found in a tumor made of thyroid follicles.
Krukenberg tumors are metastatic and bilateral in about 70 percent, which does not fit a thyroid only mass.
questions.explanation: Step 1. A tumor made almost entirely of thyroid follicles is struma ovarii. Step 2. The lecture places it among teratomas, which are germ cell tumors, as a specialized monodermal type that contains only thyroid elements. A related variant, strumal carcinoid, contains thyroid tissue and carcinoid tissue. A single tissue type does not make it a sex cord tumor.
visual_clues: Trace several epithelial rims. The pink material is luminal across multiple follicles.
questions.visual_target: Colloid filled follicles of thyroid type

questions.tested_concept: What does this well differentiated cartilage imply about the tumor's behavior?
questions.visual_target: Mature cartilage as a separate ovarian tissue pattern
questions.scenario: A 24-year-old woman has an incidental 8 cm right ovarian cystic mass. A section from a different teaching specimen of this kind shows isolated chondrocytes in lacunae within a broad matrix, along with skin elements.
questions.lead_in: What does this well differentiated cartilage imply about the tumor's behavior?
questions.stem: What does this well differentiated cartilage imply about the tumor's behavior?
options: It supports a Krukenberg tumor from a gastrointestinal primary with bilateral masses
It supports an immature teratoma that needs prophylactic chemotherapy after surgery
It supports a dysgerminoma that is responsive to chemotherapy and radiation
It supports a mature cystic teratoma, benign in more than 90 percent of cases
It supports a granulosa cell tumor with estrogen secretion and hyperplasia
choice_rationales: Krukenberg tumors have signet ring cells and a gastrointestinal primary.
Immature teratoma requires primitive tissue such as neuroepithelium, not mature cartilage.
Dysgerminoma is a sheet like proliferation of large primitive cells.
Mature, well differentiated tissue is the hallmark of the benign mature cystic teratoma.
Granulosa cell tumors are sex cord stromal tumors with Call-Exner bodies.
questions.explanation: Step 1. Mature cartilage with chondrocytes in lacunae, combined with skin elements, shows differentiation into multiple tissues, which is a mature cystic teratoma. Step 2. The lecture states that more than 90 percent of teratomas are benign mature cystic teratomas. Malignant transformation is rare and usually to squamous cell carcinoma, whereas immature teratomas contain primitive tissue such as neuroepithelium.
visual_clues: Rounded cells lie in lacunae in a continuous matrix.
questions.ground_truth_basis: Visible findings in the cited learner image interpreted with the cited teaching pages.
questions.condition_overview: Mature cystic teratoma is the most common ovarian germ cell tumor and is benign. It is a unilocular cyst lined by skin with sebaceous glands and hair follicles, containing hair and greasy sebum and often teeth, bone, cartilage, thyroid, and brain tissue derived from all three germ layers. It is a frequent cause of adnexal masses in young women, is bilateral in about 10 to 15 percent, and can cause torsion or, rarely, autoimmune anti-NMDA receptor encephalitis. A rare complication is malignant transformation to squamous cell carcinoma. Imaging shows fat that loses signal on fat suppression.

questions.tested_concept: Which complication would be most likely in the older patient?
questions.visual_target: Gross cavity and squamous lining in a separate ovarian specimen
questions.scenario: A 29-year-old woman has a pelvic mass. At surgery a right ovarian cyst is opened. The cavity is lined by a stratified squamous epithelium, with sebaceous secretion inside. Years later, a 60-year-old woman with an untreated lesion of this type develops a mass in the wall.
questions.lead_in: Which complication would be most likely in the older patient?
questions.stem: Which complication would be most likely in the older patient?
options: Transformation to a dysgerminoma
Spontaneous progression to extramammary Paget disease of the vulva, which is the usual late complication of a cyst
Conversion to a granulosa cell tumor, a sex cord stromal tumor that commonly develops from the cyst lining in older women
Development of a Krukenberg tumor
Malignant transformation, usually to squamous cell carcinoma
choice_rationales: Dysgerminoma is a separate pure germ cell tumor.
Paget disease is a vulvar intraepidermal lesion.
Granulosa cell tumors are sex cord stromal tumors and are a different lineage.
Krukenberg tumors are metastases and do not arise from a dermoid cyst.
Malignant change in a dermoid cyst is usually squamous cell carcinoma, arising from the squamous lining.
questions.explanation: Step 1. A cyst lined by stratified squamous epithelium with sebaceous secretion is a mature cystic teratoma (dermoid cyst), about 90 percent unilateral and more often on the right. Step 2. The lecture notes that malignant transformation can occur and is usually to squamous cell carcinoma, which would be suspected when a mass develops in the wall of a long standing lesion.
visual_clues: A grossly open cavity is paired with a stratified squamous lining.

questions.scenario: A 17-year-old woman has a rapidly growing pelvic mass and a serum alpha fetoprotein of 2,400. A section from the tumor shows a vascular core wrapped by tumor cells that projects into a space.
questions.lead_in: Which tumor does this structure indicate, and how does the AFP result fit?
questions.stem: Which tumor does this structure indicate, and how does the AFP result fit?
options: Krukenberg tumor, whose signet ring cells produce alpha fetoprotein
Granulosa cell tumor, whose Call-Exner bodies and inhibin production explain the elevated alpha fetoprotein in this patient
Mature cystic teratoma, whose chondrocytes produce alpha fetoprotein
Yolk sac tumor, whose cells produce alpha fetoprotein and form Schiller-Duval bodies
Dysgerminoma, whose large cells in sheets with lymphocytic septa produce the elevated alpha fetoprotein found in this patient
choice_rationales: Krukenberg tumors are mucin rich metastases and are not AFP tumors.
Granulosa cell tumors are marked by inhibin, not AFP.
Benign mature teratoma does not secrete AFP from cartilage.
Schiller-Duval bodies and AFP elevation define yolk sac tumor.
Dysgerminoma has large cells in sheets with lymphocytic septa and is not the AFP secreting tumor.
questions.explanation: Step 1. A papilla with a central vessel covered by tumor cells and projecting into a space is a Schiller-Duval body, characteristic of yolk sac tumor. Step 2. The lecture lists elevated alpha fetoprotein as the laboratory finding and alpha fetoprotein positivity on immunostains, with hyaline PAS positive bodies containing AFP. The tumor is a germ cell tumor of young women and children.
visual_clues: Locate the cluster of red cells near the center.
Follow the rim of tumor around the vessel and the space outside that rim.

questions.condition_overview: Yolk sac (endodermal sinus) tumor is a malignant germ cell tumor, the most common testicular tumor in infants and children, and it occurs in young women in the ovary. Microscopically a loose reticular or lacelike pattern of cuboidal cells surrounds open spaces. Schiller-Duval bodies are glomerulus-like structures with a central vessel surrounded by tumor cells within a space, and eosinophilic hyaline globules are common. Tumor cells secrete alpha-fetoprotein, which is a serum marker. It is chemosensitive.

questions.scenario: A 22-year-old woman has a large pelvic mass. Her serum AFP is high and hCG is normal. Immunostains on the tumor are positive for alpha fetoprotein, glypican 3, SALL4, and cytokeratin.
questions.lead_in: Which diagnosis is supported, and which marker would instead point to embryonal carcinoma?
questions.stem: Which diagnosis is supported, and which marker would instead point to embryonal carcinoma?
options: Dysgerminoma, whereas embryonal carcinoma is characterized by inhibin positivity
Struma ovarii, whereas embryonal carcinoma is characterized by thyroglobulin positivity
Yolk sac tumor, whereas embryonal carcinoma is characterized by CD30 and OCT3/4 positivity
Immature teratoma, whereas embryonal carcinoma is characterized by calponin positivity
Granulosa cell tumor, whereas embryonal carcinoma is characterized by AFP positivity
choice_rationales: Dysgerminoma does not stain for AFP, and inhibin is a granulosa marker.
Struma ovarii is thyroid tissue and does not have these germ cell markers.
Yolk sac tumor is AFP and glypican 3 positive, and embryonal carcinoma is CD30 and OCT3/4 positive.
Immature teratoma is defined by primitive tissue and calponin marks myoepithelium.
Granulosa cell tumor is inhibin positive and is not the AFP tumor described here.
questions.explanation: Step 1. Positivity for AFP, glypican 3, SALL4, and cytokeratin in a germ cell tumor with high AFP is a yolk sac tumor. Step 2. The lecture lists embryonal carcinoma with keratin, CD30, OCT3/4, NANOG, SALL4, and SOX2 positivity, so CD30 and OCT3/4 help separate it from yolk sac tumor, which is AFP and glypican 3 positive.
visual_clues: Distinguish the blood filled core from the outer space around the projection.

questions.condition_overview: Yolk sac (endodermal sinus) tumor is a malignant germ cell tumor, the most common testicular tumor in infants and children, and it occurs in young women in the ovary. Microscopically a loose reticular or lacelike pattern of cuboidal cells surrounds open spaces. Schiller-Duval bodies are glomerulus-like structures with a central vessel surrounded by tumor cells within a space, and eosinophilic hyaline globules are common. Tumor cells secrete alpha-fetoprotein, which is a serum marker. It is chemosensitive.

questions.scenario: A pathologist examines a yolk sac tumor and is surprised to see a loose reticular network around irregular spaces in one area and solid sheets and glandular areas in another.
questions.lead_in: What explains the variety of architectural patterns in the same tumor?
questions.stem: What explains the variety of architectural patterns in the same tumor?
options: The patterns recapitulate stages of yolk sac development, including reticular, myxoid, solid and glandular forms
Epidermal invasion has occurred, so the tumor has become a mixed squamous tumor of the ovary
The tumor is a metastatic signet ring tumor with variable amounts of intracellular mucin
The tumor has transformed into a granulosa cell tumor with Call-Exner bodies in the stroma
Different tumors have collided in the ovary, because yolk sac tumors never show more than one pattern
choice_rationales: The lecture lists multiple patterns that mirror yolk sac development.
Yolk sac tumors are germ cell tumors and are not squamous epithelial lesions.
Signet ring cells have intracellular mucin vacuoles and a gastrointestinal primary.
Granulosa tumors are sex cord stromal tumors, and one tumor type does not convert into another here.
The lecture describes a range of patterns in a single yolk sac tumor, not collision of separate tumors.
questions.explanation: Step 1. A loose reticular network with irregular spaces is one pattern of yolk sac tumor. Step 2. The lecture states that its microscopic patterns recapitulate yolk sac development and include reticular, myxoid, solid, glandular, and polyvesicular forms, along with Schiller-Duval bodies and hyaline PAS positive bodies. Several patterns can therefore coexist in a single tumor.

questions.scenario: A 19-year-old woman has primary amenorrhea and a streak gonad on one side. She now has a unilateral, solid, gray, soft ovarian mass. A biopsy shows sheets of large cells separated by fibrous septa that contain small dark lymphocyte nuclei.
questions.lead_in: Which tumor is this, and what clinical association does the lecture give?
questions.stem: Which tumor is this, and what clinical association does the lecture give?
options: Embryonal carcinoma, with CD30 positive cells, necrosis and elevated hCG in young adults
Dysgerminoma, the most common malignant germ cell tumor, 5 to 10 percent with gonadal dysgenesis
Yolk sac tumor, with elevated AFP, Schiller-Duval bodies and hyaline globules in the tumor
Granulosa cell tumor, with estrogen effects, inhibin positivity and Call-Exner bodies
Krukenberg tumor, with signet ring cells, intracellular mucin and bilateral ovarian masses
choice_rationales: Embryonal carcinoma is crowded, atypical epithelium with necrosis.
Dysgerminoma matches the septa, the age, and the gonadal dysgenesis association.
Yolk sac tumor is recognized by Schiller-Duval bodies and AFP, not lymphoid septa.
Granulosa tumors are estrogenic sex cord tumors.
Krukenberg tumors are bilateral signet ring metastases.
questions.explanation: Step 1. Sheets of large primitive cells separated by fibrous septa infiltrated by lymphocytes is a dysgerminoma, the analog of seminoma. Step 2. The lecture says it is the most common malignant ovarian germ cell tumor, most often under age 30, can be seen in pregnancy, is responsive to chemotherapy, and is associated with gonadal dysgenesis in 5 to 10 percent. The streak gonad and amenorrhea point to that association.
visual_clues: The small lymphocytes cluster in a fibrous septum between groups of large pale cells.

questions.condition_overview: Dysgerminoma is the ovarian counterpart of testicular seminoma and the most common malignant ovarian germ cell tumor, typically in young women. It forms a solid, pale, fleshy, lobulated mass. Microscopically large round cells with clear cytoplasm, distinct cell borders, and central nuclei with prominent nucleoli are arranged in nests separated by fibrous septa infiltrated by lymphocytes. Cells are OCT3/4, CD117, and PLAP positive. Tumors are highly radiosensitive and chemosensitive with an excellent prognosis. It can occur in gonadal dysgenesis, such as Swyer syndrome.

questions.condition_overview: Embryonal carcinoma is an aggressive malignant germ cell tumor of the testis and, rarely, the ovary, composed of primitive epithelial cells in glands, papillae, and solid sheets with crowded, overlapping, pleomorphic nuclei and frequent necrosis and hemorrhage. Cells express CD30 and cytokeratin and OCT3/4. The cut surface is variegated with hemorrhagic and necrotic areas. It spreads hematogenously and lymphatically and is a component of many mixed germ cell tumors. Treatment is orchiectomy and chemotherapy.

questions.scenario: A 34-year-old woman has vaginal bleeding at 10 weeks, a uterus larger than dates, and a markedly elevated hCG. Evacuated tissue from her case is compared with a second patient's specimen. In her tissue (left) nearly all villi are broadly enlarged with prominent circumferential trophoblast. In the second specimen (right) enlarged villi are mixed with small, fibrotic villi with scalloped borders.
questions.lead_in: Which diagnoses fit the two fields, and which follow up applies to the left case?
questions.stem: Which diagnoses fit the two fields, and which follow up applies to the left case?

Left is a normal placenta and right a partial mole, with no hCG follow up after evacuation
Left is a partial mole and right a complete mole, and no follow up is needed afterward
Both are invasive moles with deep myometrial invasion, and hCG is followed because they embolize to the lungs
Both are placenta accreta with absent decidua and villous attachment to the myometrium, with hysterectomy as the follow up
choice_rationales: Diffusely enlarged villi indicate a complete mole, and hCG surveillance is needed for persistent disease and choriocarcinoma.
A normal placenta would not have diffusely hydropic villi, and hCG surveillance is needed.
The patterns are reversed in this option.
Invasive mole requires penetration of the myometrium, which is not shown in these fields.
Placenta accreta is an abnormally adherent placenta without decidua, and not a molar villous pattern.
questions.explanation: Step 1. Uniformly dilated villi with circumferential trophoblast proliferation are a complete mole, while two populations of villi with scalloping and trophoblastic inclusions are a partial mole. Step 2. The lecture states that up to 10 percent of moles become persistent or invasive and 2.5 percent of complete moles evolve into gestational choriocarcinoma, so serum hCG is followed until it falls to and remains at normal. Partial moles also carry a 5 to 10 percent risk of persistent disease.

Dark cellular rims are more striking on the left.

questions.condition_overview: A complete hydatidiform mole is a diploid (usually 46,XX) androgenetic conception in which all chromosomes are paternal, so there is no fetal tissue. All chorionic villi are diffusely enlarged, edematous (hydropic), with a central cistern and circumferential trophoblastic hyperplasia. The uterus is distended with grapelike vesicles, hCG is markedly elevated, and ultrasound shows a snowstorm pattern. p57 is negative because the maternal gene is absent. It is treated by suction curettage with hCG follow-up because 15 to 20 percent develop persistent gestational trophoblastic disease.

questions.stem: Which pair matches the morphologic patterns, and what genetics explain each?

Both are partial moles that are 46,XX and androgenetic and lack any fetal parts
First is a choriocarcinoma from fetal tissue, and second is a normal placenta with villi
First is a complete mole, usually 46,XX by sperm duplication, and second a triploid partial mole
Both are complete moles that are 69,XXY and have both maternal and paternal chromosomes
choice_rationales: The patterns and genetics are reversed in this option.
Androgenesis defines complete moles, not partial moles.
Choriocarcinoma is a malignant trophoblastic tumor and not a vesicular specimen.
Complete moles are androgenetic and partial moles are triploid from dispermy.
Triploidy defines partial moles, not complete moles.
questions.explanation: Step 1. Grape like vesicles with no embryo are a complete mole, whereas an embryo with mixed villi and inclusions is a partial mole. Step 2. The lecture states that a complete mole arises when an egg that has lost its chromosomes is fertilized and the genetic material is wholly paternal (90 percent 46,XX from one sperm duplicating, the rest from two sperm), whereas partial moles result from two sperm fertilizing one egg and are triploid, for example 69,XXY.

Smooth muscle nodules of leiomyomas that distend the cavity of the uterus and bleed
Embryonic tissue growing in the uterine tube and distending its wall with chorionic villi

questions.condition_overview: A partial hydatidiform mole is usually triploid (69,XXY), from fertilization of one egg by two sperm, and an embryo or fetal parts are often present. Two populations of villi occur: large hydropic villi with scalloped borders and trophoblastic inclusions, and small normal-appearing villi, with only focal mild trophoblast hyperplasia. p57 is positive because the maternal genome is present. It carries a much lower risk of persistent trophoblastic disease than a complete mole and is treated with curettage and hCG follow-up.

questions.scenario: A 29-year-old woman had a complete mole evacuated 3 months ago. Her hCG plateaus, and she has persistent bleeding. A hysterectomy specimen shows hydropic villi lying between bundles of myometrial muscle.
questions.lead_in: What does this finding indicate, and what risk accompanies it?
questions.stem: What does this finding indicate, and what risk accompanies it?
options: Invasive mole, locally destructive, which may invade parametrial tissue and vessels and embolize to the lungs and brain
Adenomyosis from endometrial glands lying within the muscular wall of the uterus
A leiomyoma with hydropic degeneration within the myometrium of the uterus
A complete mole that has stayed in the cavity, with hydropic villi lifting off the endometrium and needing only repeat evacuation
Placenta accreta, with normal villi adherent to the myometrium because decidua is absent, treated by hysterectomy without chemotherapy
choice_rationales: Hydropic villi inside myometrium define invasive mole with local destruction and embolization.
Adenomyosis has endometrial glands and stroma, not hydropic villi.
A leiomyoma is a smooth muscle tumor and does not contain villi.
Hydropic villi penetrating between muscle bundles show myometrial invasion, so this is not a mole confined to the cavity.
Placenta accreta is normal placental tissue adherent to myometrium without decidua, whereas hydropic villi with trophoblastic proliferation indicate a mole.
questions.explanation: Step 1. Hydropic villi penetrating between myometrial muscle bundles is an invasive mole (chorioadenoma destruens), a mole that penetrates or perforates the uterine wall. Step 2. The lecture states the tumor is locally destructive, may invade parametrial tissue and blood vessels, and hydropic villi may embolize to distant sites such as the lung and brain but do not grow there. Up to 10 percent of moles become persistent or invasive.
visual_clues: Hydropic villi lie between myometrial smooth muscle bundles.

questions.condition_overview: An invasive mole is a hydatidiform mole in which hydropic villi penetrate the myometrium and may involve vessels. Villous structure is preserved, which separates it from choriocarcinoma. It follows evacuation of a complete mole in a minority of cases and presents with persistent or rising hCG and bleeding. It is a form of gestational trophoblastic neoplasia that is treated with chemotherapy and usually responds well.

questions.explanation: Step 1. An empty egg fertilized by one sperm that duplicates gives a 46,XX diploid complement entirely paternal (androgenesis), the commonest origin of a complete mole. Step 2. questions.condition_overview: Invasive ductal carcinoma, no special type, is the most common breast cancer (about 75 percent). It presents as a hard, irregular, fixed mass with stellate borders that may cause skin dimpling or nipple retraction. Cords, nests, and glands of atypical cells infiltrate a desmoplastic stroma. It is graded by tubule formation, nuclear grade, and mitotic rate, and receptor status (ER, PR, HER2) guides therapy. It spreads to axillary nodes, bone, lung, liver, and brain.

questions.condition_overview: Invasive lobular carcinoma is the second most common breast cancer. Small, discohesive cells with intracytoplasmic mucin infiltrate in single files (Indian files) and targetoid patterns around normal ducts, often without a discrete mass, and it can be missed on imaging. questions.condition_overview: Lichen sclerosus is a chronic, probably autoimmune inflammatory skin disorder that mainly affects the vulva and perianal skin of postmenopausal women and also the penis (balanitis xerotica obliterans). Patients have intense itching and white, thin, parchment-like plaques that cause architectural change such as loss of labia minora and a narrowed introitus. Microscopically the epidermis is thin with loss of rete ridges, the superficial dermis is pale and homogenized (sclerotic), and a band of lymphocytes lies beneath it. It carries a small increased risk of vulvar squamous cell carcinoma, so persistent or ulcerated areas are biopsied. First-line therapy is a potent topical corticosteroid.

Biopsy of persistent lesions excludes lichen sclerosus and vulvar intraepithelial neoplasia.

questions.condition_overview: Condyloma acuminatum is a benign, exophytic anogenital wart caused by low-risk human papillomavirus (mainly types 6 and 11). It appears as single or multiple raised, rough, cauliflower-like papules. Microscopically there are papillary fronds of acanthotic squamous epithelium over fibrovascular cores, with hyperkeratosis and koilocytes (cells with enlarged wrinkled nuclei and perinuclear clearing) in the upper layers. Condylomata are transmitted sexually, are not generally premalignant, and are treated by ablation, topical therapy, or excision. HPV vaccination prevents most cases.

questions.condition_overview: Condyloma acuminatum is a benign, exophytic anogenital wart caused by low-risk human papillomavirus (mainly types 6 and 11). It appears as single or multiple raised, rough, cauliflower-like papules. Microscopically there are papillary fronds of acanthotic squamous epithelium over fibrovascular cores, with hyperkeratosis and koilocytes (cells with enlarged wrinkled nuclei and perinuclear clearing) in the upper layers. Condylomata are transmitted sexually, are not generally premalignant, and are treated by ablation, topical therapy, or excision. HPV vaccination prevents most cases.

questions.condition_overview: Differentiated VIN is an HPV-independent precancer of the vulva that occurs in older women and is typically associated with lichen sclerosus. The atypia is confined to the basal and parabasal layers, with premature keratinization and maturing, eosinophilic superficial cells that make it easy to overlook. Mutated p53 is often present. dVIN is the usual precursor of HPV-independent keratinizing vulvar squamous cell carcinoma and progresses rapidly, so it is excised.

questions.condition_overview: Papillary hidradenoma is a benign tumor of the anogenital (mammary-like) sweat glands that forms a small, well-circumscribed, often asymptomatic nodule in the dermis of the vulva. Microscopically it shows branching papillary and tubular glands lined by two cell layers, an inner luminal layer and an outer myoepithelial layer (highlighted by calponin or p63), within a fibrous stroma. It resembles intraductal papilloma of the breast and can be mistaken for adenocarcinoma, but it is benign and cured by excision.

questions.condition_overview: Cervical intraepithelial neoplasia (CIN) is HPV-driven dysplasia of the cervical squamous epithelium graded by the depth of epithelium replaced by atypical cells (CIN 1 lower third, CIN 2 two thirds, CIN 3 full thickness). At colposcopy, application of acetic acid whitens areas with dense nuclear protein (acetowhite epithelium) because of a high nuclear-to-cytoplasmic ratio. Lugol iodine fails to stain dysplastic cells because they lack glycogen, giving a mustard-yellow area. These findings guide biopsy. Higher grades are treated by excision or ablation to prevent invasive carcinoma.

It is LSIL (CIN I), and vaccines can clear an established HPV infection of the cervix
It is Paget disease of the cervix, and vaccines protect against this intraepithelial cancer
It is LSIL, and HPV types 16 and 18 are never involved in lesions of this kind
It is invasive carcinoma, since the surface epithelium of the cervix is involved by the lesion

CIN I is LSIL and is limited to the lower third.
Paget disease is vulvar and is unrelated to HPV vaccination.
HPV 16 and 18 account for about half of HSIL.
Invasive carcinoma requires invasion into the underlying stroma.
questions.explanation: Step 1. Full thickness atypia with no maturation is HSIL (CIN III). Step 2. The lecture states HPV types 16 and 18 account for about half of HSILs, and that vaccines made of L1 capsid protein protect against these types but cannot protect against established infections, so screening continues. Invasion needs stromal penetration, not surface involvement alone.

questions.condition_overview: High-grade squamous intraepithelial lesion (HSIL, CIN 2 and CIN 3) is the true cervical precancer. It arises from persistent infection with high-risk HPV (types 16 and 18 most often), in which viral E6 and E7 proteins inactivate p53 and Rb. Immature basaloid cells with high nuclear-to-cytoplasmic ratios, hyperchromatic nuclei, and mitoses occupy at least the lower two thirds up to the full thickness of the epithelium, with loss of maturation toward the surface. Diffuse strong p16 staining supports the diagnosis. HSIL is treated by excision or ablation because it can progress to invasive squamous cell carcinoma.

questions.condition_overview: Low-grade squamous intraepithelial lesion (LSIL, CIN 1) is a productive HPV infection of the cervical squamous epithelium. Atypical cells with koilocytic change are confined mainly to the lower third of the epithelium, and the upper layers mature normally. It most often reflects low- or high-risk HPV, usually regresses spontaneously, especially in young women, and is generally followed rather than treated aggressively. On Pap smear the finding is koilocytes with mildly enlarged hyperchromatic nuclei in superficial and intermediate cells.

questions.condition_overview: Adenomyosis is the presence of benign endometrial glands and stroma within the myometrium, deeper than the usual endometrial-myometrial junction. The uterus enlarges symmetrically and has a thickened, trabeculated wall with small cystic or hemorrhagic foci. Patients have heavy, painful menses and a boggy, tender uterus. Microscopically there are islands of endometrial-type glands with stromal cuffs among smooth muscle bundles, with hypertrophy of the surrounding muscle. On MRI it thickens the junctional zone. Definitive treatment is hysterectomy.

questions.condition_overview: Uterine leiomyomas (fibroids) are benign smooth muscle tumors and the most common tumor in women, growth being estrogen and progesterone dependent. They are classified as submucosal (beneath the endometrium, causing the most bleeding), intramural (within the wall), or subserosal (beneath the serosa, causing pressure effects). They are well-circumscribed, firm, whorled, white-tan masses with interlacing bundles of uniform spindle cells without atypia. Symptoms include heavy menstrual bleeding, pelvic pressure, and infertility, and they shrink after menopause. Malignant transformation (leiomyosarcoma) is rare.

questions.condition_overview: Endometriosis is the presence of functional endometrial glands and stroma outside the uterus, most often on the ovaries, pelvic peritoneum, and rectovaginal septum, and rarely in the bladder, vagina, or even the lung. Ectopic tissue responds to cyclic hormones, bleeds, and causes chronic inflammation and fibrosis. Patients have dysmenorrhea, pelvic pain, dyspareunia, and infertility. Ovarian involvement forms endometriomas (chocolate cysts) filled with old blood. Microscopically two of three elements are needed: endometrial glands, stroma, and hemosiderin-laden macrophages. Catamenial symptoms, such as thoracic or bladder symptoms with menses, suggest distant implants.

questions.condition_overview: Mature cystic teratoma is the most common ovarian germ cell tumor and is benign. It is a unilocular cyst lined by skin with sebaceous glands and hair follicles, containing hair and greasy sebum and often teeth, bone, cartilage, thyroid, and brain tissue derived from all three germ layers. It is a frequent cause of adnexal masses in young women, is bilateral in about 10 to 15 percent, and can cause torsion or, rarely, autoimmune anti-NMDA receptor encephalitis. The vulvar skin, since the cells are Paget cells that contain mucin and spread to the ovary
The thyroid, since the vacuoles are colloid that lies within the follicles of the thyroid
The germ cells of the other ovary, since the cells are components of a teratoma
The uterine myometrium, since the cells are endometrial in origin and spread by contiguity
choice_rationales: Krukenberg tumors most often come from a gastrointestinal primary, especially gastric.
Paget cells are vulvar, not ovarian metastases.
Thyroid follicles contain colloid, not signet ring vacuoles.
A teratoma is a primary germ cell tumor, not a mucin rich metastasis.
Endometrial cells do not form this pattern in the lecture.
questions.explanation: Step 1. Mucin rich cells with intracellular vacuoles displacing the nucleus are signet ring cells, and bilateral ovarian involvement defines Krukenberg tumor. Step 2. The lecture states Krukenberg tumors are metastatic signet ring adenocarcinomas, from a gastrointestinal primary in about 70 percent of cases (gastric origin is typical), and can also arise from colon, breast, appendix, and biliary tract. Her epigastric symptoms point to the stomach.

questions.condition_overview: Krukenberg tumor is a metastasis to the ovary, usually bilateral, from a mucin-producing adenocarcinoma, most often of the stomach, and also the colon or breast. The ovaries are enlarged and nodular. Microscopically, signet-ring cells with intracytoplasmic mucin displacing the nucleus infiltrate a cellular, reactive ovarian stroma, often with mucin pools. A benign dermoid cyst with hair, sebum and mature tissue from all three germ layers, which is usually unilateral and cystic
A primary sex cord tumor with Call-Exner bodies and inhibin positive tumor cells
A primary serous carcinoma with papillary growth, psammoma bodies and high grade nuclei that is often bilateral
A primary germ cell tumor with Schiller-Duval bodies, hyaline globules and elevated AFP

Dermoid cysts contain hair and differentiated tissue.
Call-Exner bodies define granulosa cell tumor.
Serous carcinoma is papillary and does not have intracellular mucin vacuoles.
Schiller-Duval bodies define yolk sac tumor, not signet ring cells.

questions.lead_in: What does the distribution add?

Bilateral masses prove the primary tumor is in the uterus and has spread to both ovaries
Bilateral masses favor a mature cystic teratoma, since about 90 percent of mature teratomas are bilateral and multinodular in young women
Bilateral masses favor a dysgerminoma, since most dysgerminomas are bilateral and multinodular in young women with an elevated LDH
Bilateral masses favor a granulosa cell tumor, since most granulosa tumors are bilateral

Bilaterality does not by itself prove a uterine primary.
Mature cystic teratomas are about 90 percent unilateral.
Dysgerminomas are typically unilateral.
Granulosa cell tumors are mostly unilateral.

The lecture states about 70 percent of metastatic ovarian cancers are bilateral with multiple nodules, whereas dysgerminoma and granulosa cell tumor are mostly unilateral and about 90 percent of dermoid cysts are unilateral. questions.visual_target: A separate metastatic growth pattern in ovarian stroma
questions.scenario: A 55-year-old woman had a lobular carcinoma of the breast treated years ago. She now has an ovarian mass. A section of the ovarian mass shows small cells infiltrating the ovarian stroma in narrow single files with little stromal reaction, unlike the large pale vacuolated signet ring cells of a gastric metastasis.
questions.lead_in: Which origin is most likely, and why is this primary a more frequent ovarian metastasis than ductal carcinoma?
questions.stem: Which origin is most likely, and why is this primary a more frequent ovarian metastasis than ductal carcinoma?
options: Breast, since metastatic breast cancer is mostly bilateral and lobular reaches the ovary more than ductal (36 vs 2.6 percent)
Yolk sac, since single files of cells indicate Schiller-Duval bodies within the ovary of a young woman
Stomach, since the single file pattern is a signet ring cell pattern from the gastric mucosa
Granulosa cells, since single files of small cells indicate Call-Exner bodies, and these tumors are mostly bilateral
Thyroid, since single file small cells indicate struma ovarii, which spreads to the ovary more often than ductal cancer
choice_rationales: Lobular breast cancer metastasizes to the ovary far more often than ductal cancer and keeps its single file pattern.
Schiller-Duval bodies are vascular papillae of yolk sac tumor.
Gastric metastases show mucin rich signet ring cells, not single file small cells.
Call-Exner bodies are follicle like structures of granulosa cell tumor and not single file infiltration with little stromal response.
Struma ovarii is thyroid follicles with colloid and not single file lobular infiltration, and it is not a metastasis.
questions.explanation: Step 1. Narrow single file infiltration with little stromal response is the lobular (Indian file) pattern, so a metastasis from lobular breast carcinoma is expected. Step 2. The lecture states breast cancer accounts for about 40 percent of metastatic ovarian cancers, usually bilateral (about 80 percent), histologically similar to the primary, and lobular carcinoma metastasizes more often than ductal carcinoma (36 percent versus 2.6 percent). Krukenberg tumors are signet ring tumors from the gastrointestinal tract.
visual_clues: Small tumor cells infiltrate ovarian stroma in narrow linear files.

questions.scenario: A 58-year-old woman with recurrent E. coli urinary tract infections has soft yellow plaques on cystoscopy. A biopsy shows foamy histiocytes containing rounded, dense, laminated inclusions at the two arrows.
questions.lead_in: What do these inclusions represent, and what failure in the macrophages produces them?
questions.stem: What do these inclusions represent, and what failure in the macrophages produces them?
options: Michaelis-Gutmann bodies, mineralized remnants of partially digested bacteria from poor macrophage killing
Schiller-Duval bodies, papillary structures from yolk sac tumor differentiation in the ovary
Koilocytes, cells with enlarged nuclei and perinuclear halos from HPV infection of squamous cells
Signet ring vacuoles, mucin that displaces the nucleus of adenocarcinoma cells in the bladder
Call-Exner bodies, follicle like structures within granulosa cell tumor cells of the ovary
choice_rationales: Michaelis-Gutmann bodies are mineralized debris in macrophages with defective bacterial killing.
Schiller-Duval bodies are yolk sac tumor structures in the ovary.
Koilocytes are squamous cells showing HPV effect.
Signet ring cells are tumor cells in Krukenberg tumor.
Call-Exner bodies are found in granulosa cell tumors.
questions.explanation: Step 1. Foamy histiocytes with basophilic, laminated, mineralized inclusions are Michaelis-Gutmann bodies, the hallmark of malakoplakia. Step 2. The lecture explains the pathogenesis as insufficient killing of bacteria by macrophages, so partially digested bacteria accumulate with deposition of iron and calcium. This explains the link with chronic bacterial infection.
visual_clues: Trace the arrows to the rounded dense bodies among the pink cells.

questions.condition_overview: Malakoplakia is a chronic inflammatory condition, most often of the bladder, caused by defective bacterial killing by macrophages, usually with Escherichia coli infection. Soft yellow-tan plaques form on the mucosa. Microscopically sheets of foamy, granular histiocytes (von Hansemann cells) contain round, targetoid, laminated, calcified Michaelis-Gutmann bodies. It is treated with antibiotics that penetrate macrophages.

questions.stem: What is the diagnosis, and what treatment does the lecture list?

Chronic cystitis, treated by catheter removal
Endometriosis of the bladder, treated with hormones
Invasive urothelial carcinoma, treated with BCG
Malakoplakia, an inflammatory condition, treated with antibiotics

Chronic cystitis shows chronic inflammation, fibrosis, and metaplasia without Michaelis-Gutmann bodies.
Bladder endometriosis contains endometrial glands, stroma, and hemosiderin laden macrophages.
Invasive urothelial carcinoma shows tumor nests and cords in the wall, not histiocytes.
The lecture identifies malakoplakia as an inflammatory condition treated with antibiotics.

Soft plaques with foamy histiocytes and Michaelis-Gutmann bodies in a patient with infection is malakoplakia, a rare chronic inflammatory condition that is not neoplastic. Step 2. questions.stem: Why does this gross pattern direct the biopsy, and what is expected histologically?
options: Soft yellow plaques are typical of malakoplakia, with foamy histiocytes and Michaelis-Gutmann bodies
Plaques are typical of schistosomiasis, expected to show only squamous carcinoma of the bladder
Plaques are typical of papillary urothelial carcinoma, expected to show fibrovascular fronds
Pale plaques are typical of squamous hyperplasia, expected to show glycogen rich squamous cells
Plaques are typical of carcinoma in situ, expected to show cohesive normal appearing urothelium

Schistosomiasis is a risk factor for squamous carcinoma and does not describe these histiocytes.
Papillary carcinoma forms projecting fronds, not flat plaques.
Squamous hyperplasia is a vulvar lesion and is not what the lecture describes here.
Carcinoma in situ is velvety and poorly cohesive, not a plaque with histiocytes.

questions.tested_concept: What is the best interpretation, and how does it differ from acute cystitis?

questions.scenario: A 70-year-old woman with a long term indwelling catheter has frequent bladder symptoms. A cystitis biopsy shows lamina propria containing eosinophils, plasma cells, lymphocytes, and rare neutrophils under an unremarkable urothelium. Her urine is negative for pyuria.
questions.lead_in: What is the best interpretation, and how does it differ from acute cystitis?
questions.stem: What is the best interpretation, and how does it differ from acute cystitis?
options: Chronic cystitis with chronic inflammation and fibrosis, whereas acute cystitis has edema and neutrophils
Acute suppurative cystitis with a purulent exudate and abundant neutrophils in the bladder wall
Invasive carcinoma with tentacular cords of cells infiltrating the detrusor muscle
Malakoplakia with Michaelis-Gutmann bodies within foamy histiocytes of the lamina propria
Urothelial carcinoma in situ with poorly cohesive markedly atypical cells on the surface
choice_rationales: Chronic inflammatory cells and fibrosis define chronic cystitis, versus edema and acute cells in acute cystitis.
Suppurative cystitis has a purulent exudate and pyuria, which is absent.
Invasive carcinoma needs tumor infiltration of the wall.
Malakoplakia needs foamy histiocytes with Michaelis-Gutmann bodies.
Carcinoma in situ is a high grade atypical flat lesion, and the urothelium here is unremarkable.
questions.explanation: Step 1. A lamina propria infiltrate of lymphocytes, plasma cells, and eosinophils with few neutrophils is chronic cystitis. Step 2. The lecture lists chronic inflammatory cells and fibrosis with squamous metaplasia or urothelial hyperplasia, and subtypes such as papillary or polypoid from long term indwelling catheters, whereas acute cystitis has edema, congestion, and acute inflammatory cells (suppurative, hemorrhagic, and others).
visual_clues: The dense small inflammatory cells are beneath the lining in the lamina propria.

questions.condition_overview: Chronic cystitis is long-standing bladder inflammation from recurrent infection, stones, or irritation. The bladder mucosa is red and granular, and the lamina propria contains a dense infiltrate of lymphocytes and plasma cells, with sometimes lymphoid follicles. Symptoms are urgency, frequency, and dysuria. Treatment is directed at the cause.

questions.scenario: A 67-year-old man with a 40 pack year smoking history has painless gross hematuria. A transurethral resection shows tumor nests interdigitating with broad bundles of smooth muscle.
questions.lead_in: What does this finding mean for his prognosis and management?
questions.stem: What does this finding mean for his prognosis and management?
options: Muscularis propria invasion, a high stage tumor needing more than local resection, with stage the key prognostic factor
It shows endometriosis, which is treated with hormonal therapy and surgical excision
It shows only superficial disease, so repeat resection and follow up are sufficient
It shows a benign inflammatory process of foamy histiocytes, treated with a prolonged course of antibiotics
It shows carcinoma in situ confined to the urothelium, treated with intravesical BCG alone and surveillance
choice_rationales: Muscle invasion is high stage disease and staging drives prognosis.
Endometriosis consists of endometrial glands and stroma and not tumor nests in muscle.
Low grade, superficial tumors are the ones managed by follow up and resection.
Antibiotics treat malakoplakia, not tumor nests among muscle bundles.
BCG is used for high grade tumors that are non invasive or superficially invasive, whereas nests among muscle bundles are muscle invasion.
questions.explanation: Step 1. Tumor nests among broad muscle bundles are invasion of the detrusor, which is invasive urothelial carcinoma. Step 2. The lecture states that extent of invasion at diagnosis (staging) is the most important prognostic factor. Low grade tumors are followed and resected, high grade superficial tumors receive resection with BCG or chemotherapy, and high grade tumors with muscle invasion need more aggressive treatment. Smoking is a listed risk factor.
visual_clues: Follow the pink bundles and find dark tumor between adjacent bundles.

questions.condition_overview: Invasive urothelial carcinoma grows beyond the urothelial basement membrane into the lamina propria and, in more advanced disease, the muscularis propria (detrusor), perivesical fat, and beyond. Irregular nests and cords of atypical cells infiltrate between smooth muscle bundles with a desmoplastic stroma. Depth of invasion, especially muscle invasion, is the most important prognostic factor. Muscle-invasive disease is treated by radical cystectomy with neoadjuvant chemotherapy, and urine cytology alone cannot determine depth.

questions.scenario: A 72-year-old man has a bladder tumor. At another field the tumor below the surface shows slender irregular cords of cells infiltrating the underlying stroma in thin finger like strands.
questions.lead_in: Which description from the lecture matches this pattern, and what does it imply about spread?
questions.stem: Which description from the lecture matches this pattern, and what does it imply about spread?
options: Tentacular pattern of invasive urothelial carcinoma, spreading by local extension into nearby tissue
Simple papillary architecture of a low grade papillary neoplasm with normal looking cytology and no invasion
Foamy histiocytes with calcified inclusions as seen in malakoplakia, with no invasive pattern in the wall
A cohesive dome shaped dermal nodule as seen in hidradenoma, which spreads by local extension of its cells
Endometrial glands with hemosiderin laden macrophages as seen in endometriosis spreading to the bladder
choice_rationales: Thin cords invading diffusely are described as the tentacular pattern of invasive carcinoma.
Simple papillary architecture with normal cells describes a noninvasive neoplasm.
Malakoplakia is a histiocytic inflammatory plaque.
Hidradenoma is a vulvar dermal nodule.
Endometriosis is a benign condition of endometrial glands and stroma.

Urothelial carcinoma tends to spread by local extension to surrounding tissues, so infiltrating cords in the stroma indicate invasion beyond the surface. Noninvasive papillary lesions have simple papillary architecture without invasion.
visual_clues: Follow individual dark cords down from the surface region.

The tumor is a metastasis from the ovary that has spread to the bladder wall
The tumor is confined to the urothelium, so it is carcinoma in situ

questions.scenario: A 69-year-old man has urinary irritation and positive urine cytology, but cystoscopy shows only a velvety red patch without a mass. A flat biopsy shows marked atypia in a flat urothelial lining with poorly cohesive cells.
questions.lead_in: What can this biopsy establish compared with the deep tumor biopsy?
questions.stem: What can this biopsy establish compared with the deep tumor biopsy?
options: A flat high grade lesion, carcinoma in situ, without a mass, unlike an invasive tumor with muscle involvement
A metastasis from the stomach spread to the bladder surface, with signet ring cells in a flat mucosa
An adenocarcinoma of the bladder base arising from glandular metaplasia
A low grade papillary neoplasm that recurs in 45 percent of patients
A benign inflammatory plaque of foamy histiocytes with calcified Michaelis-Gutmann inclusions in the bladder wall
choice_rationales: Flat, velvety, poorly cohesive high grade atypia without a mass defines CIS.
Gastric metastasis would show signet ring cells, whereas flat velvety high grade atypia without a mass is carcinoma in situ.
Adenocarcinoma is mucin producing glandular tumor, which is not described.
Low grade papillary tumors have mild atypia and a papillary architecture.
Malakoplakia is made of foamy histiocytes with inclusions and does not show high grade atypia in a flat urothelium.
questions.explanation: Step 1. Marked atypia in a flat, velvety, poorly cohesive urothelium without a mass is flat urothelial carcinoma in situ, a high grade lesion. Step 2. The lecture contrasts it with papillary tumors and with invasive carcinoma, which invades the detrusor, so this biopsy shows high grade cytology but does not by itself show invasion. High grade lesions are managed with resection and BCG or chemotherapy if non or superficially invasive.

questions.condition_overview: Urothelial carcinoma in situ is a flat, high-grade noninvasive malignancy in which markedly atypical cells with large hyperchromatic pleomorphic nuclei replace the urothelium without papillae. It appears as red velvety patches, causes irritative symptoms, and cells are often shed into urine, so cytology is usually positive. It often progresses to muscle-invasive disease if untreated, and standard therapy is intravesical BCG.

questions.scenario: A 66-year-old man has a papillary bladder tumor. A biopsy shows papillary architecture, marked variation in nuclear size and shape, frequent mitoses, and necrosis. The sample is small and does not include the underlying wall.
questions.lead_in: Which inference does the field support, and what remains unproven?
questions.stem: Which inference does the field support, and what remains unproven?
options: High grade papillary urothelial carcinoma, with coexistent invasion the small sample cannot exclude
Malakoplakia, with Michaelis-Gutmann bodies in foamy histiocytes of the bladder wall forming a papillary necrotic mass
Low grade papillary carcinoma, which almost never invades the bladder wall at diagnosis and needs only surveillance
A benign papilloma with cytologically normal cells lining thin fibrovascular fronds
A papillary urothelial neoplasm of uncertain malignant potential with no atypia

Malakoplakia is an inflammatory plaque and has no necrotic papillary tumor.
Low grade tumors have mild atypia and under 10 percent coexistent invasion.
Cytologically normal cells describe a low risk lesion, not this one.
A neoplasm of uncertain potential lacks marked atypia.
questions.explanation: Step 1. Marked cytologic atypia, frequent mitoses, and necrosis in a papillary tumor define high grade papillary urothelial carcinoma. Step 2. The lecture states up to 80 percent have coexistent invasion, compared with under 10 percent for low grade, so depth must be assessed by adequate sampling that includes muscle. Grade is established by nuclear features and architecture, whereas stage requires the wall.
visual_clues: The nuclei vary markedly in size and shape, and the cells lose orderly polarity.

questions.condition_overview: Papillary urothelial carcinoma is the most common bladder cancer pattern and forms exophytic fronds with fibrovascular cores covered by urothelium. Low-grade tumors show orderly layering with mild nuclear atypia, while high-grade tumors show marked nuclear pleomorphism, mitoses, disordered polarity, and often necrosis. Smoking and certain chemicals are major risk factors, and patients have painless hematuria. Low-grade tumors recur often but rarely invade, whereas high-grade tumors can invade the muscle wall and metastasize. Treatment is transurethral resection, with BCG for high-risk non-muscle-invasive disease.

questions.scenario: A 71-year-old man has hematuria. A urine specimen from a comparison case shows clusters of atypical urothelial cells with enlarged irregular nuclei. The urologist asks what this proves.
questions.lead_in: Which conclusion should be carried forward?
questions.stem: Which conclusion should be carried forward?
options: The atypical cells support malignancy, but invasion depth must still be shown by tissue biopsy
The cytology proves that the tumor is benign and that no further workup is needed
The cytology establishes an ovarian primary that has spread to the bladder, so a gynecologic work up replaces cystoscopy
The cytology identifies malakoplakia by Michaelis-Gutmann bodies in the cells
The cytology establishes muscle invasion and the stage of the bladder tumor, so a tissue biopsy is unnecessary for staging
choice_rationales: Cytology supports malignancy, and depth still requires biopsy.
Atypical cells with irregular nuclei are not benign.
Cytology of urine cannot assign an ovarian origin.
Malakoplakia is identified by foamy histiocytes in tissue.
Urine cells cannot show invasion of muscle.
questions.explanation: Step 1. Atypical urothelial cells with enlarged irregular nuclei in urine support urothelial carcinoma. Step 2. The lecture lists urine cytology and tests such as FISH, ImmunoCyt, and NMP22 as diagnostic aids, but staging, meaning depth of invasion, is the most important prognostic factor and needs cystoscopic biopsy. Cytology cannot show wall depth.
visual_clues: Dark atypical urothelial cells with large nuclei relative to their cytoplasm support concern for malignancy.

questions.condition_overview: Papillary urothelial carcinoma is the most common bladder cancer pattern and forms exophytic fronds with fibrovascular cores covered by urothelium. Low-grade tumors show orderly layering with mild nuclear atypia, while high-grade tumors show marked nuclear pleomorphism, mitoses, disordered polarity, and often necrosis. Smoking and certain chemicals are major risk factors, and patients have painless hematuria. Low-grade tumors recur often but rarely invade, whereas high-grade tumors can invade the muscle wall and metastasize. Treatment is transurethral resection, with BCG for high-risk non-muscle-invasive disease.

The glands are normal peripheral zone glands expected to be negative

Benign glands retain basal cells, so negativity is abnormal.

questions.condition_overview: Prostatic adenocarcinoma is the most common nonskin cancer in men and typically arises in the peripheral zone, so it presents late with urinary symptoms and is often found by PSA or digital rectal examination. Small crowded glands infiltrate between benign glands and stroma, lined by a single layer of cells with prominent nucleoli, and the basal cell layer is absent (p63 and high-molecular-weight keratin negative), while AMACR is often positive. Grading uses the Gleason system by glandular architecture: pattern 3 well-formed glands, pattern 4 fused or cribriform glands, and pattern 5 solid sheets, cords, or single cells with comedonecrosis. questions.scenario: A pathologist integrates a stain field containing larger rimmed glands and smaller atypical glands without rims. The patient, a 70-year-old man, has a firm irregular nodule in the peripheral prostate and PSA 14. He asks if the cancer is likely to cause urinary obstruction early.
questions.lead_in: Which statement correctly interprets the two gland populations and the clinical presentation?
questions.stem: Which statement correctly interprets the two gland populations and the clinical presentation?
options: Rim loss supports invasion, and since 70 to 80 percent of cancers are peripheral they obstruct less than BPH
Rim loss supports normal glands and requires no biopsy of the prostate
Rim loss indicates a metastasis of a testicular germ cell tumor to the prostate
Rim loss supports BPH, which arises in the peripheral zone and obstructs the urethra early, so the rim loss is a benign finding
Rim loss is expected in all benign glands of the transition zone, so the PSA is unreliable and no biopsy of the prostate is needed
choice_rationales: Loss of basal cells supports cancer, and peripheral origin explains delayed obstruction.
Missing basal cells are abnormal and require diagnosis.
Testicular germ cell tumors are unrelated to prostatic basal cells.
BPH arises centrally and periurethrally, not peripherally.
Benign glands retain basal cells.
questions.explanation: Step 1. The smaller atypical glands lack basal cells, which supports invasive adenocarcinoma. Step 2. The lecture states 70 to 80 percent of prostate cancers arise in the outer peripheral glands and are less likely than BPH to cause urethral obstruction early. BPH involves the central gland and periurethral transition zone, which is why it obstructs. A PSA of 10 or greater and a firm irregular nodule are expected findings.

Large glands with papillary infolding and a preserved double cell layer

questions.scenario: A 62-year-old man has a prostate biopsy showing atypical epithelium with enlarged nuclei and prominent nucleoli forming projections within a recognizable ductal outline. A basal cell marker still highlights an outer layer around this duct.
questions.lead_in: What does the retained ductal outline and basal layer suggest about this lesion?
questions.stem: What does the retained ductal outline and basal layer suggest about this lesion?
options: It is confined within a duct, as in prostatic intraepithelial neoplasia, so not invasive, though often with cancer
It is a seminoma, because large nuclei with prominent nucleoli are present in the cells
It is invasive adenocarcinoma, because atypia is present in the lining cells
It is malakoplakia, because the duct contains foamy histiocytes with inclusions, so it is a benign inflammatory lesion
It is BPH, because the lining shows crowded cells with a preserved basal layer, so no further follow up is required
choice_rationales: Atypia within an intact duct with basal cells is noninvasive and is often found with cancer.
Seminoma is a testicular germ cell tumor and is not a prostate lesion.
Invasive cancer lacks basal cells, which are retained here.
Malakoplakia is a histiocytic inflammatory condition, whereas this duct contains atypical epithelium with a preserved basal layer.
Simple hyperplasia lacks nuclear atypia, whereas atypia confined to an intact duct is high grade PIN, which is often found with cancer and needs follow up.
questions.explanation: Step 1. Atypical epithelium confined within an intact duct with a preserved outer basal layer is a noninvasive precursor type of lesion, consistent with high grade PIN. Step 2. The lecture states that 80 percent of cancer cases show high grade PIN, and that invasive cancer lacks basal cells, so retained basal cells argue against invasion here. The inference about the duct outline follows from that principle.
visual_clues: The abnormal epithelium projects inward into a recognizable preexisting duct.

questions.lead_in: Where is this layer located?
questions.stem: Where is this layer located?
options: At the outer edge of each gland beside the stroma, beneath the luminal secretory cells
In the center of each gland lumen, as the secretory layer that faces the luminal space
Within the periurethral glands only, and not within the glands of the peripheral zone
In the lumen of the gland, as crystalloids secreted from the glandular cells themselves
Within the stroma as scattered histiocytes that surround the prostatic glands at the margin
choice_rationales: Basal cells lie outside the secretory layer, adjacent to the stroma.
The secretory cells face the lumen, not the basal cells.
Basal cells are not limited to the periurethral glands.
Crystalloids may be seen in cancer secretions and are not a cell layer.
Histiocytes are inflammatory cells and are not basal cells.
questions.explanation: Step 1. Benign prostate glands are lined by secretory cells with basal cells lying at the outer edge beside the stroma (yellow arrows in the lecture figure). Step 2. Because the basal layer is absent in invasive adenocarcinoma, locating it in benign glands is the basis of immunostains such as CK903. Cancer glands have a single luminal cell layer.

questions.scenario: A 29-year-old man with a history of cryptorchidism has a painless testicular swelling. An orchiectomy specimen shows a bulky, homogeneous, grey white to cream colored, lobulated mass with pale fleshy lobules, with little hemorrhage or necrosis.
questions.lead_in: What does this gross appearance predict about behavior and treatment?
questions.stem: What does this gross appearance predict about behavior and treatment?
options: Seminoma, usually limited by the tunica albuginea, radiosensitive and highly curable
Leydig cell tumor, which is yellow, usually benign and causes hormonal effects
Yolk sac tumor, which is cystic and AFP negative with a poor response to treatment
Embryonal carcinoma, which is necrotic and aggressive and spreads through the blood
Choriocarcinoma, which is hemorrhagic and radioresistant and spreads through the blood
choice_rationales: Homogeneous fleshy cut surface without necrosis fits seminoma, which is radiosensitive and curable.
Leydig cell tumors are sex cord tumors and are not the typical germ cell mass.
Yolk sac tumor is a different germ cell tumor, and AFP is elevated.
Embryonal carcinoma shows necrosis and is more aggressive.
Choriocarcinoma is hemorrhagic and not described as a pale homogeneous mass.
questions.explanation: Step 1. A bulky, homogeneous, fleshy cream to tan lobulated mass with rare hemorrhage and necrosis is a seminoma. Step 2. The lecture states it is the most common testicular germ cell tumor in ages 15 to 40, usually limited by the tunica albuginea, radiosensitive with a high cure rate, and history of cryptorchidism in 10 percent. Embryonal carcinoma is more aggressive and often metastatic, with necrosis.

questions.condition_overview: Seminoma is the most common testicular germ cell tumor, in men aged 15 to 45. It forms a homogeneous, pale tan-white, fleshy, bulging mass. Microscopically sheets or nests of uniform large cells with clear glycogen-rich cytoplasm, distinct cell borders, and round central nuclei with prominent nucleoli are separated by fibrous septa with lymphocytes. Cells express OCT3/4, CD117, and PLAP. It is highly radiosensitive and has an excellent prognosis, and it commonly arises in undescended testes.
