questions.scenario: A 33-year-old man has a painless testicular mass. A biopsy shows the tissue pattern of nests of large cells with lymphocytes. Immunostains are positive for OCT3/4 and CD117, and serum beta hCG is mildly elevated.
questions.lead_in: Which diagnosis does this integrate, and how can a mild hCG rise be explained?
questions.stem: Which diagnosis does this integrate, and how can a mild hCG rise be explained?
options: Seminoma, in which syncytiotrophoblasts occur in about 15 percent of cases and can raise hCG
Spermatocytic tumor, since it is OCT3/4 positive and has three cell sizes
Sertoli cell tumor, since it is CD117 positive and forms tubules in a stroma
Choriocarcinoma, since any hCG elevation always means choriocarcinoma of the testis
Yolk sac tumor, since OCT3/4 marks yolk sac cells and hCG is secreted by the tumor
choice_rationales: Seminoma can contain syncytiotrophoblasts that raise hCG modestly.
Spermatocytic tumor is OCT3/4 negative and lacks lymphocytes.
Sertoli cell tumors are sex cord tumors and do not match germ cell markers.
Choriocarcinoma needs trophoblastic tumor morphology, and hCG alone is not diagnostic.
Yolk sac tumor is AFP positive, not OCT3/4 positive.
questions.explanation: Step 1. Nests of large cells with lymphocytes and OCT3/4 and CD117 positivity are a seminoma. Step 2. The lecture states that beta hCG positivity occurs in about 15 percent of cases from syncytiotrophoblasts, so a mild hCG rise does not by itself change the diagnosis. Spermatocytic tumor is distinct, being CD117 and SALL4 positive but PLAP and OCT3/4 negative, with no lymphocytes, granulomas, or GCNIS.

Grooved oval nuclei with small follicle like structures of the Call-Exner type
Spindle cells with central nuclei arranged in whorls and fascicles
Indistinct borders with vacuolated cytoplasm pushing the nucleus to the side of the cell
Small dark cells with scant cytoplasm and no nucleoli arranged in sheets

Grooved nuclei with follicles describe granulosa cell tumor.
Spindle cells in whorls describe a stromal tumor.
Peripheral nuclei in vacuolated cells describe signet ring cells.
Small dark cells with scant cytoplasm do not match the large clear cells.
questions.explanation: Step 1. The lecture describes seminoma cells as having distinct membranes, clear or light cytoplasm, and a large central nucleus with a prominent nucleolus, arranged in nests divided by fibrous bands with lymphocytes. Step 2. Signet ring cells have peripheral nuclei, spindle cells with central nuclei describe thecoma or fibroma, and grooved nuclei with follicles describe granulosa cell tumor, so the cytology separates seminoma from these.

questions.lead_in: Why does this gross pattern argue against a pure seminoma?
questions.stem: Why does this gross pattern argue against a pure seminoma?
options: Hemorrhage and necrosis suggest a nonseminomatous germ cell tumor such as embryonal carcinoma, more aggressive and often metastatic
Hemorrhage and necrosis are expected in seminoma, which looks homogeneous only after fixation
Dark and pale areas show a spermatocytic tumor of an older man, which is more aggressive than seminoma and often metastatic
Dark and pale areas show a Sertoli cell tumor, a sex cord stromal tumor that is hormonally active and usually metastatic
Dark and pale areas show a benign Leydig cell tumor with golden brown tissue
choice_rationales: Variegated hemorrhagic, necrotic tumors favor nonseminomatous types such as embryonal carcinoma.
Hemorrhage and necrosis are rare in seminoma.
Spermatocytic tumor occurs in older men and is indolent, so it does not explain hemorrhage and necrosis or aggressive spread.
Sex cord stromal tumors are usually benign, so they do not account for a hemorrhagic, necrotic, metastatic tumor.
A Leydig cell tumor is a sex cord tumor and does not account for metastasis here.
questions.explanation: Step 1. Seminoma is a homogeneous, fleshy mass with rare hemorrhage and necrosis. Step 2. questions.scenario: A 28-year-old man with cryptorchidism has a testicular biopsy from tissue next to his tumor. The field shows large atypical cells lining a recognizable seminiferous tubule, with no invasion into the stroma. The cells stain for PLAP.
questions.lead_in: What does this boundary distinguish, and why does it matter?
questions.stem: What does this boundary distinguish, and why does it matter?
options: Intratubular germ cell neoplasia (GCNIS) within a tubule, the precursor of most germ cell tumors
Invasive seminoma already spreading through the testicular stroma and tunica albuginea
A benign Sertoli cell tumor of the sex cord stroma forming tubules
A spermatocytic tumor that is unrelated to GCNIS and occurs in older men
Malakoplakia of the testis with foamy histiocytes and Michaelis-Gutmann bodies
choice_rationales: A tubule encircling atypical germ cells is intratubular germ cell neoplasia, the precursor lesion.
Invasive seminoma would extend into stroma, which is absent here.
Sertoli cell tumors are sex cord tumors and do not stain with PLAP.
Spermatocytic tumor is PLAP negative and unrelated to GCNIS.
Malakoplakia is a histiocytic condition of the urinary tract.
questions.explanation: Step 1. Large atypical cells confined within a recognizable seminiferous tubule and positive for PLAP are intratubular germ cell neoplasia (GCNIS). Step 2. The lecture states most germ cell tumors are preceded by intratubular germ cell neoplasia, and that cryptorchidism increases risk three to five times. PLAP stains germ cell tumors and intratubular neoplasia, whereas spermatocytic tumor is unrelated to GCNIS and is PLAP negative.
visual_clues: The large abnormal cells stay within the contour of a seminiferous tubule.

questions.condition_overview: Germ cell neoplasia in situ (GCNIS) is the precursor lesion of most testicular germ cell tumors. Large atypical cells with clear cytoplasm, large nuclei, and prominent nucleoli line the base of seminiferous tubules next to the basement membrane, and they stain for PLAP, OCT3/4, and CD117. Risk factors include cryptorchidism and gonadal dysgenesis. It can progress to invasive tumors over years.

questions.condition_overview: Seminoma is the most common testicular germ cell tumor, in men aged 15 to 45. It forms a homogeneous, pale tan-white, fleshy, bulging mass. Spiculated masses from invasive lobular carcinoma, which commonly shows calcifications and infiltrates in single files
Sound transmission through cysts that are filled with clear fluid on ultrasound
Smooth rounded masses from fibroadenoma with a pushing border and mobile edges
Fat necrosis from a prior injury, since calcifications occur there, so grouped branching foci need no further evaluation

Lobular carcinoma induces little stromal response, has no calcifications, and can be mammographically occult.
Cysts are described by sonography with sound transmission.
Fibroadenomas are round circumscribed masses, with popcorn calcifications only when older.
Fat necrosis can cause calcifications, but grouped fine branching or linear calcifications are the hallmark of DCIS and need evaluation.

questions.condition_overview: Invasive ductal carcinoma, no special type, is the most common breast cancer (about 75 percent). It presents as a hard, irregular, fixed mass with stellate borders that may cause skin dimpling or nipple retraction. Cords, nests, and glands of atypical cells infiltrate a desmoplastic stroma. questions.condition_overview: Serous tubal intraepithelial carcinoma (STIC) is a noninvasive precursor lesion of high-grade serous carcinoma found in the fallopian tube, usually in the fimbria. Crowded, stratified secretory cells with enlarged hyperchromatic nuclei, loss of polarity, and mitoses replace the normal lining, with a strongly aberrant p53 pattern and high Ki-67. It is often found in women with BRCA mutations. This led to opportunistic salpingectomy as a risk-reducing strategy.

questions.condition_overview: Serous tubal intraepithelial carcinoma (STIC) is a noninvasive precursor lesion of high-grade serous carcinoma found in the fallopian tube, usually in the fimbria. Crowded, stratified secretory cells with enlarged hyperchromatic nuclei, loss of polarity, and mitoses replace the normal lining, with a strongly aberrant p53 pattern and high Ki-67. It is often found in women with BRCA mutations. This led to opportunistic salpingectomy as a risk-reducing strategy.

questions.scenario: A 35-year-old woman with a BRCA1 variant has completed childbearing. Her clinicians compare two operations. Operation A removes both fallopian tubes and leaves both ovaries. Operation B removes both tubes and ovaries (risk reducing salpingo-oophorectomy). She asks which is useful given the tubal location of precursor lesions.
questions.lead_in: Which implication follows from comparing the two operations?
questions.stem: Which implication follows from comparing the two operations?
options: Operation A removes possible tubal precursor tissue and spares the ovaries, but only B is proven to cut mortality in carriers
Operation A is proven to cut mortality in carriers more than operation B, since it removes the tubes
Operation B leaves the tubes in place and preserves the ovaries, so it cuts ovarian cancer risk in carriers
Operation A raises the risk of ovarian cancer because the ovaries stay in place and continue to make estrogen after the tubes are removed
Neither operation changes the ovarian cancer risk because tubal precursor lesions are never found in women who carry BRCA variants
choice_rationales: Salpingectomy removes tubal precursors and preserves the ovaries, while only BSO is proven to reduce carrier mortality.
The lecture says RRSO is the only intervention proven to reduce mortality in carriers.
Operation B removes both the tubes and the ovaries.
Removing the tubes lowers, not raises, serous ovarian cancer risk.
Opportunistic salpingectomy was associated with a lower risk of serous ovarian cancer.
questions.explanation: Step 1. Many high grade serous cancers have a tubal STIC precursor, so removing the tubes eliminates a potential source while leaving the ovaries in place (opportunistic salpingectomy). Step 2. The lecture states that risk reducing BSO is the only intervention proven to reduce ovarian cancer specific mortality in BRCA carriers, with about an 80 percent reduction in ovarian and tubal cancer risk, so operation A is an option for lowering risk in the general population but does not replace RRSO in carriers.
visual_clues: Row A removes both tubes and leaves both ovaries.

questions.stem: Which gross combination in the ovarian specimen would support an ovarian primary, and how does this explain her effusions?
options: Solid irregular tissue with cavities and papillary surfaces, indicating epithelial ovarian cancer spread to the pleura
A smooth thin walled cyst with clear fluid, indicating a benign follicular cyst that causes pleural effusions
A uniformly yellow mass with no cavities, indicating a thecoma that always causes pleural effusions
A tiny normal ovary with no mass, indicating that pleural metastases arise from a vulvar primary
A hair containing cyst with sebum, indicating a mature teratoma that commonly spreads to the pleura
choice_rationales: Solid papillary tissue with cavities is a malignant epithelial ovarian pattern linked to effusions.
A smooth thin walled cyst with clear fluid is benign and does not fit.
Thecomas are benign estrogenic stromal tumors.
A normal ovary would not explain the pelvic masses.
Mature teratomas are usually benign and unilateral.
questions.explanation: Step 1. Solid, irregular tissue with cavities and papillary surfaces on the ovary is typical of epithelial ovarian carcinoma (serous type), which is about 90 percent of ovarian cancers. Step 2. Epithelial ovarian cancer commonly spreads through the peritoneal cavity, explaining abdominal bloating and effusions, and cytology of the fluid can show papillary clusters. This fits the case packet's picture of an older woman with bloating and effusions.
visual_clues: The lesion has a substantial solid component with irregular papillary appearing surfaces and cavities.

questions.condition_overview: Epithelial ovarian cancer arises from the ovarian surface epithelium or fallopian tube and includes serous, endometrioid, clear cell, and mucinous types. It is often silent until advanced, with ascites and omental disease. Ultrasound shows complex solid and cystic masses with papillary projections, and CA-125 is often elevated. Staging is surgical, and treatment is cytoreductive surgery with platinum-based chemotherapy.

questions.stem: Given this immunostain panel, which lineage is most likely and which site should be evaluated for a primary tumor?
options: Mesothelial lineage; evaluate the pleura.
Colorectal epithelial lineage; evaluate the colon.
Pulmonary epithelial lineage; evaluate the lung.
Renal epithelial lineage; evaluate the kidneys.
Müllerian epithelial lineage; evaluate the adnexa.
choice_rationales: Calretinin is negative, so the panel offers less support for mesothelial lineage. The combined positive pattern favors Müllerian epithelium. This choice describes mesothelioma.
CDX2 is negative, weakening the colorectal alternative. The positive PAX8 and CA125 pattern fits the Müllerian workup. This choice describes colorectal adenocarcinoma.
TTF1 is negative, and the combined panel fits Müllerian origin better than a pulmonary primary. Pleural fluid is the sampling site. This choice describes lung adenocarcinoma.

PAX8 can occur in renal as well as Müllerian tissue. PAX8 alone cannot establish renal origin, and the other positive markers and follow-up favor the adnexa. This choice describes renal cell carcinoma.

CK7, PAX8 and CA125 positivity together favor Müllerian lineage, prompting evaluation of the adnexa. This choice describes a Müllerian (ovarian or tubal serous) carcinoma, which is what the image shows.
questions.explanation: Step 1. Immunostains narrow lineage before they identify a precise anatomic primary. Step 2. In this case the panel supported Müllerian carcinoma and ovarian follow-up established the primary. PAX8 alone would not distinguish an ovarian source from a renal or other PAX8-positive source.
visual_clues: CK7, PAX8, and CA125 are positive.

questions.scenario: A 75-year-old man has a weak urinary stream, nocturia, and an enlarged prostate and undergoes transurethral resection. Two tissue fields are shown.
questions.lead_in: Which finding supports the hyperplastic component, and why does this tissue cause his symptoms?
questions.condition_overview: Benign prostatic hyperplasia (BPH) is a nodular proliferation of glands and stroma in the periurethral transition zone, driven by dihydrotestosterone and increasing with age. Enlarged nodules compress the prostatic urethra, causing hesitancy, weak stream, nocturia, and incomplete emptying, with risks of retention, infection, and bladder hypertrophy. Microscopically there are large glands with papillary infoldings with two cell layers, and basal cells are preserved. It does not become cancer. Treatment is with alpha-blockers, 5-alpha-reductase inhibitors, or resection.

questions.visual_target: Focal crowded glands in a prostate resection
questions.stem: How does this field change the interpretation of the resection?
options: It raises concern for adenocarcinoma, needing basal cell marker staining since cancer glands lack a basal layer
It suggests adenocarcinoma, but basal cell staining is not needed because cancer glands retain a basal layer
It is consistent with benign hyperplasia since the glands retain a basal layer, so no further testing is needed
It proves bladder cancer because atypical cells are seen, so no staining of the prostate is needed
It proves malakoplakia because foamy cells are seen, so no staining of the gland is required to exclude carcinoma
choice_rationales: A suspicious focus with lost dual layering needs basal cell stains to rule out carcinoma.
Cancer glands lack a basal layer, so basal cell marker staining is the test that confirms the concern.
The field raises concern for adenocarcinoma, and basal cell staining is needed to show the basal layer is absent.
Bladder cancer is a different organ.
Malakoplakia is a histiocytic condition.
questions.explanation: Step 1. Crowded small glands that lose their dual cell layering are suspicious because prostate adenocarcinoma shows small single layer glands with the basal layer missing. Step 2. The lecture states 70 to 80 percent of cancers arise in the peripheral zone, but a focus can occur in resections, and basal cell markers such as CK903 or p63 plus AMACR are used to confirm. The hyperplasia explanation still stands for the obstruction but does not exclude carcinoma.
visual_clues: Compare the crowded left-sided profiles with glands that retain an apparent outer layer.

questions.condition_overview: Menopause is the permanent end of menstruation after 12 months of amenorrhea, at an average age of about 51, caused by depletion of ovarian follicles. questions.condition_overview: Menopause is the permanent end of menstruation after 12 months of amenorrhea, at an average age of about 51, caused by depletion of ovarian follicles. Estradiol and inhibin B fall, so FSH (and later LH) rise, and the main estrogen becomes extragonadal estrone from adipose aromatization of androstenedione. Estrogen deficiency causes hot flashes, vaginal atrophy, sleep disturbance, bone loss and osteoporosis, and adverse lipid changes. Perimenopause is the preceding transition with irregular cycles, and treatment is symptomatic, including hormone therapy in selected patients.

questions.stem: Which decision is guided by the testing listed in the last row, and why does BRCA or HRD status matter?
options: Whether to perform debulking surgery, since BRCA status decides if the tumor can be resected at all
Whether to use PARP inhibitor maintenance after chemotherapy, since homologous recombination deficient tumors repair breaks poorly
Whether to screen her relatives for ovarian cancer with CA-125 alone, since BRCA status needs no genetic test
Whether to use carboplatin and paclitaxel as first line chemotherapy, since BRCA or HRD status decides which regimen is chosen and whether it is given at all
Whether to use tamoxifen after surgery, since BRCA positive tumors are estrogen receptor positive and respond to antiestrogen maintenance therapy

BRCA and HRD results guide PARP inhibitor maintenance after chemotherapy.
The lecture says ovarian cancer screening is not recommended for average risk women, and CA-125 alone is not the decision here.

questions.explanation: Step 1. The lecture lists carboplatin plus paclitaxel as the initial chemotherapy and germline and tumor testing at diagnosis. Step 2. Maintenance therapy with a PARP inhibitor (olaparib, niraparib), with or without bevacizumab, is guided by BRCA and HRD status. questions.condition_overview: Cervical squamous cell carcinoma is the most common cervical cancer and arises from persistently infected high-risk HPV lesions at the transformation zone through HSIL. Nests of malignant squamous cells with keratin pearls and intercellular bridges invade the cervical stroma. It presents with postcoital or abnormal bleeding, or may be found by screening. Staging uses tumor size, parametrial, pelvic wall, and nodal spread. Advanced disease can obstruct the ureters and cause hydronephrosis and renal failure, which is a major cause of death. Treatment is surgery for early disease and chemoradiation with brachytherapy for advanced disease.

questions.scenario: A 29-year-old woman with HSIL on Pap test undergoes colposcopy. A teaching comparison shows two panels. After Lugol iodine the arrow marks a yellow, nonstaining area next to dark brown tissue. After acetic acid the arrow marks a region that turns white.
questions.lead_in: Which paired mechanism explains the changes at the arrows?
questions.stem: Which paired mechanism explains the changes at the arrows?
options: Iodine is taken up by glycogen and abnormal cells have less, so they stay yellow, and acetic acid dehydrates cells so nuclear protein rich epithelium whitens
Iodine is taken up by abnormal cells because they hold more glycogen, and acetic acid dissolves glycogen in the normal cells
Both agents stain mucin in abnormal cells, so abnormal areas look brown with iodine and white with acetic acid
Iodine stains the keratin of the superficial layer in normal cells, and acetic acid whitens abnormal cells by dehydrating them
Iodine is taken up by glycogen in normal cells, and acetic acid whitens normal cells because they contain more nuclear protein
choice_rationales: Iodine needs glycogen and acetic acid exposes nuclear protein, so abnormal areas are yellow and acetowhite.
Normal glycogen rich cells take up iodine, not abnormal cells.
Neither agent works by staining mucin.
The lecture ties iodine uptake to glycogen and not to keratin.
Iodine uptake by glycogen is correct, but acetic acid whitens abnormal cells because they have more nuclear protein, not normal cells.
questions.explanation: Step 1. The lecture states that Lugol iodine is taken up by glycogen, and abnormal cells have less glycogen, so they appear yellow and nonstaining. Step 2. Acetic acid (vinegar) dehydrates cells, and abnormal cells with more nuclear protein turn white (acetowhite). The two stains therefore highlight different properties of dysplastic epithelium and direct the biopsy.
visual_clues: Compare the light area at the Lugol arrow with the darker adjacent tissue. The other arrow marks whitening after acetic acid.

questions.condition_overview: Cervical intraepithelial neoplasia (CIN) is HPV-driven dysplasia of the cervical squamous epithelium graded by the depth of epithelium replaced by atypical cells (CIN 1 lower third, CIN 2 two thirds, CIN 3 full thickness). At colposcopy, application of acetic acid whitens areas with dense nuclear protein (acetowhite epithelium) because of a high nuclear-to-cytoplasmic ratio. Lugol iodine fails to stain dysplastic cells because they lack glycogen, giving a mustard-yellow area. These findings guide biopsy. Higher grades are treated by excision or ablation to prevent invasive carcinoma.

questions.condition_overview: Vulvar squamous cell carcinoma has two main pathways. HPV-related tumors arise from usual-type VIN in younger women and are basaloid or warty. HPV-independent tumors arise from dVIN or lichen sclerosus in older women and are keratinizing. Keratinizing tumors show irregular nests of atypical squamous cells with keratin pearls and intercellular bridges invading dermis. Depth of invasion, tumor size, and groin node status determine stage and prognosis. Treatment is wide excision, and groin node assessment is needed when invasion exceeds 1 mm.

The patient is over 65 and the tumor is unifocal, so groin evaluation can be omitted whatever the depth of invasion
Invasion of 1 mm or less requires groin evaluation, and sentinel node biopsy is an option for a unifocal tumor over 4 cm

questions.condition_overview: Choriocarcinoma is a highly malignant tumor of trophoblast with no villi, composed of sheets of syncytiotrophoblast, cytotrophoblast, and intermediate trophoblast. It follows a hydatidiform mole, an abortion, or a normal pregnancy, or arises as a germ cell tumor of the testis or ovary. It forms a soft, dark, hemorrhagic, necrotic mass that invades the myometrium and vessels and spreads early to the lung, vagina, brain, and liver. hCG is markedly elevated. It is highly chemosensitive, and vaginal metastases should not be biopsied because they bleed.

Observe her alone, since a raised hCG after a term birth is a normal finding in the postpartum period
Treat the findings as metastasis from a breast cancer, since the lung and vagina are common sites

There is no evidence of breast disease, and the hCG is markedly elevated.

options: Sound passes through the cyst fluid with little attenuation, producing posterior enhancement behind the fluid

choice_rationales: Fluid transmits sound with little attenuation, so deeper tissue looks brighter.

A fibroadenoma is a solid lesion with internal echoes.

questions.explanation: Step 1. questions.condition_overview: Fibroadenoma is the most common benign breast tumor, typically in women under 35. It is a well-circumscribed, rubbery, freely mobile mass (breast mouse). Microscopically it combines proliferating duct-like epithelial structures with a loose cellular stroma, which can compress the glands into slit-like spaces. Growth is hormone responsive, so it may enlarge in pregnancy and regress after menopause. Risk of cancer is minimal, and management is observation or excision.

questions.condition_overview: Uterine leiomyomas (fibroids) are benign smooth muscle tumors and the most common tumor in women, growth being estrogen and progesterone dependent. They are classified as submucosal (beneath the endometrium, causing the most bleeding), intramural (within the wall), or subserosal (beneath the serosa, causing pressure effects). They are well-circumscribed, firm, whorled, white-tan masses with interlacing bundles of uniform spindle cells without atypia. Symptoms include heavy menstrual bleeding, pelvic pressure, and infertility, and they shrink after menopause. Malignant transformation (leiomyosarcoma) is rare.

questions.condition_overview: Seminoma is the most common testicular germ cell tumor, in men aged 15 to 45. It forms a homogeneous, pale tan-white, fleshy, bulging mass. Microscopically sheets or nests of uniform large cells with clear glycogen-rich cytoplasm, distinct cell borders, and round central nuclei with prominent nucleoli are separated by fibrous septa with lymphocytes. questions.condition_overview: Testicular torsion is twisting of the spermatic cord that cuts off venous and then arterial blood flow, causing sudden severe scrotal pain, a high-riding testis, and absent cremasteric reflex. It most often affects adolescents with a bell-clapper deformity. Doppler ultrasound shows reduced or absent perfusion on the affected side. Untreated torsion leads to hemorrhagic infarction (dark, swollen testis with coagulative necrosis), and salvage requires surgery within about 6 hours.

Venous dilation from a varicocele raises the pressure in the scrotum and stops arterial flow in the testis
Obstruction of the processus vaginalis by bowel from a hernia stops arterial flow to the testis in the cord
Fluid between the tunica layers from a hydrocele raises the pressure and stops arterial flow in the testis
choice_rationales: Twisting of the cord stops perfusion and the bell clapper variant predisposes.
Orchitis increases flow rather than eliminating it.
A varicocele is venous dilation and not acute pain with absent flow.
A hernia involves bowel entering the canal and does not stop testicular flow.
A hydrocele is fluid and not a twist.
questions.explanation: Step 1. In intravaginal torsion, the testis rotates and twists the spermatic cord, compromising blood flow. This is the most common type and occurs in peripubertal males. Step 2. A bell clapper deformity, failure of normal posterior anchoring by the gubernaculum, lets the testis hang freely and raises the risk, though it cannot be diagnosed ahead of time.

questions.condition_overview: Mature cystic teratoma is the most common ovarian germ cell tumor and is benign. It is a unilocular cyst lined by skin with sebaceous glands and hair follicles, containing hair and greasy sebum and often teeth, bone, cartilage, thyroid, and brain tissue derived from all three germ layers. It is a frequent cause of adnexal masses in young women, is bilateral in about 10 to 15 percent, and can cause torsion or, rarely, autoimmune anti-NMDA receptor encephalitis. A rare complication is malignant transformation to squamous cell carcinoma. Imaging shows fat that loses signal on fat suppression.

questions.condition_overview: Mature cystic teratoma is the most common ovarian germ cell tumor and is benign. questions.condition_overview: Endometriosis is the presence of functional endometrial glands and stroma outside the uterus, most often on the ovaries, pelvic peritoneum, and rectovaginal septum, and rarely in the bladder, vagina, or even the lung. Ectopic tissue responds to cyclic hormones, bleeds, and causes chronic inflammation and fibrosis. Patients have dysmenorrhea, pelvic pain, dyspareunia, and infertility. Ovarian involvement forms endometriomas (chocolate cysts) filled with old blood. Microscopically two of three elements are needed: endometrial glands, stroma, and hemosiderin-laden macrophages. Catamenial symptoms, such as thoracic or bladder symptoms with menses, suggest distant implants.

questions.condition_overview: Adenomyosis is the presence of benign endometrial glands and stroma within the myometrium, deeper than the usual endometrial-myometrial junction. The uterus enlarges symmetrically and has a thickened, trabeculated wall with small cystic or hemorrhagic foci. Patients have heavy, painful menses and a boggy, tender uterus. Microscopically there are islands of endometrial-type glands with stromal cuffs among smooth muscle bundles, with hypertrophy of the surrounding muscle. On MRI it thickens the junctional zone. Definitive treatment is hysterectomy.
